summary: Describes how to use Kerberos V5 through the GSS-API as a mechanism inside the SASL framework, which adds authentication to connection-based protocols. It replaces Section 7.2 of RFC 2222, which defined the earlier mechanism.

plainLanguage.summary: SASL is a doorway many programs use to check who you are. This note shows how to plug in Kerberos, a ticket-based ID system, so programs can accept your ticket instead of a password.

subtitle: How a client and server use Kerberos V5 through GSS-API to authenticate inside the SASL framework.

tldr.problem: Connection-based protocols that use SASL need a standard way to authenticate users with Kerberos V5, and RFC 2222 had defined only an older version of that mechanism.
tldr.mechanism: The SASL mechanism named GSSAPI has the client go first, run GSS-API context setup with Kerberos V5, then exchange one wrapped message that negotiates a security layer, buffer sizes and the authorization identity.
tldr.outcome: It replaces Section 7.2 of RFC 2222 and, together with RFC 4422, obsoletes RFC 2222. It documents known limitations: no channel bindings and more round trips than necessary.

today: RFC 4752 is a Proposed Standard and replaces Section 7.2 of RFC 2222, which it obsoletes together with RFC 4422. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Relationship to RFC 2222
sections.content:
This document describes the currently deployed SASL mechanism that uses the Kerberos V5 mechanism of the Generic Security Service API (GSS-API). The SASL mechanism name is GSSAPI, although it is specifically tied to Kerberos V5.

The RFC says plainly that the sequence has known limitations: it lacks channel bindings, and the number of round trips needed is not minimal. The SASL working group was working on a separate document to address them.

Together with RFC 4422, it obsoletes RFC 2222 in its entirety. This document replaces Section 7.2 of RFC 2222.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the new, official write-up of a way programs already log in with Kerberos tickets. It admits a few things could be better.

sections.title: The Client Side of the Exchange
sections.content:
GSSAPI is a client goes first mechanism. The client calls GSS_Init_sec_context with the Kerberos V5 mechanism, no channel bindings and a target name of the form service@hostname, where the service name comes from the protocol's profile and the host name is the server's fully qualified name. The client MUST ask for integrity, and for a security layer it MUST also request mutual authentication and sequencing. Asking for confidentiality adds a confidentiality request. If the call returns GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED, the client passes each server token back in until the context completes.

Once the context is complete, the client checks that it provides a protection level its policy allows. It then unwraps the server's next token with GSS_Unwrap. The first octet is a bit-mask of security layers the server supports and the next three octets give the maximum message size the server can receive, in network byte order. The result must be exactly 4 octets long.

The client replies with its own wrapped data: one octet naming the chosen layer, three octets for the largest message it can receive (which MUST be 0 if it supports no security layer), and then the UTF-8 authorization identity. This is wrapped with GSS_Wrap with conf_flag set to FALSE. The client may then consider the server authenticated.
sections.plainLanguage: The program shows its ticket, waits until the server shows its own, then sends a small sealed note saying how careful to be and who it wants to act as.

sections.title: The Server Side of the Exchange
sections.content:
A server MUST NOT advertise GSSAPI unless it has acceptor credentials for the Kerberos V5 mechanism. It passes the client's first response to GSS_Accept_sec_context, returning each output token as a challenge while the call returns GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED. Servers SHOULD use a credential for the no-name case and the Kerberos V5 OID, and MAY use GSS_C_NO_CREDENTIAL or credentials for their own principal names.

When the context is established, the server SHOULD verify that the negotiated mechanism is really Kerberos V5, and if not, SASL authentication MUST be aborted. If it used the no-name credential, it SHOULD also check that the target name the client used matches the expected service name forms.

The server then sends 4 octets, wrapped with GSS_Wrap and conf_flag FALSE: a bit-mask of supported security layers followed by its maximum receive size (0 if it supports no layer). It unwraps the client's reply, checks that the chosen layer was offered and that the client's buffer size is 0 if no layer was chosen, and verifies that the authenticated source name is authorized to act as the authorization identity. That ends authentication; no additional data is expected with the success indicator.
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks that the ticket is real and for the right door, then asks what kind of security the visitor wants and whether the visitor is allowed to act as who they claim.

sections.title: Security Layers
sections.content:
Three bit-masks describe the security layer: 1 for no security layer, 2 for integrity protection (the sender calls GSS_Wrap with conf_flag FALSE) and 4 for confidentiality protection (conf_flag TRUE). Other bit-masks may be defined in the future, and bits that are not understood must be negotiated off.

When decoding received data with GSS_Unwrap, any major status other than GSS_S_COMPLETE MUST be treated as a fatal error. SASL negotiates the maximum output message size, and implementations can use GSS_Wrap_size_limit to work out the matching maximum input size.
sections.plainLanguage: After login you can choose no extra protection, tamper-proof seals on every message, or sealed and scrambled messages so nobody can read them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
When building the target name, the client SHOULD NOT canonicalize the server's fully qualified domain name using an insecure or untrusted directory service.

For compatibility with deployed software, the channel bindings parameter to both GSS-API context calls must be NULL, so GSS-API channel bindings cannot be used. The RFC expects channel bindings in SASL to be supported through a new GSS-API family of SASL mechanisms in a future document. Further considerations are in the SASL and GSS-API specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: A client should not ask an untrusted phone book for the server's real name, because a liar could point it at the wrong door.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2222
sections.content:
RFC 2222 relied on an older GSS-API version, RFC 2078, which had no integrity flag to pass in. Integrity was always requested. Because RFC 4422 requires the security layer negotiation to be integrity protected where possible, and the spec moved to RFC 2743, clients must now request integrity so that they can use GSS_Wrap on the negotiation.

The RFC does not require the mechanism to offer the integrity security layer, only that the negotiation be wrapped. It also notes that RFC 2222 implementations will not work with GSS-API implementations that require the integrity flag to be true, and that no such implementations are believed to exist.

IANA modified the existing registration for GSSAPI, listing it as not a family of mechanisms and intended for common use.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rules always asked for seals on the setup messages by habit. The new rules ask for it on purpose, so the setup cannot be tampered with.
